groups.title: How impact is counted
groups.explainer: Accounting choices that apply to every charity. Evaluators make these choices differently, and each changes who gets credit for an outcome. The evaluator view uses each evaluator's own choice.

groups.title: Exchange rates between causes
groups.explainer: Charities do different kinds of good: raising incomes, adding years of healthy life, sparing animals pain, making people more satisfied with their lives. To rank them on one list, everything is counted in one yardstick: the good of doubling one person's income for a year. (GiveWell calls this a "unit of value"; one unit is one year of doubled income.) The rates below convert a year of healthy life, a day of an animal's pain and a gain in life satisfaction into that yardstick. Change them and the ranking changes; that is the point.

groups.title: Moral weights
groups.explainer: How much one kind of good counts against another, such as saving a life against raising incomes. These are value judgments, not facts. Defaults follow the evaluator a model was imported from.

groups.title: Timing
groups.explainer: How much less good done in the future counts than the same good done today.

rows.label: Count staff's below-market pay as a donation
rows.explainer:
Many nonprofit staff earn less than they could in comparable for-profit jobs. That gap is a donation in kind: the staff pay part of the cost of the impact. When this is on, the cost of the work is cash spending plus that forgone salary, so your dollar is credited with only its share of the impact.

When it's off, as in GiveWell's and ACE's models, all of the impact is credited to cash donations. Each model estimates its own staff costs and pay gap, and says how.

rows.label: Give each charity full credit for outcomes it shares with others
rows.explainer:
Most outcomes need several organisations: a corporate pledge follows campaigns by several groups. Off (the default, and ACE's approach) credits each charity with its estimated share. On credits each with the whole outcome, on the view that removing any necessary link would have stopped it.

Shares never add up across charities under full credit, so comparisons between charities that share outcomes get harder. Use it to see how much a ranking depends on the choice.

rows.label: A year of healthy life, in years of doubled income
rows.technical: Units of value per DALY (disability-adjusted life year) averted
rows.explainer:
How many years of doubling one person's income a year of healthy life is worth. It lets health programmes, which add healthy years, sit on the same list as everything else.

A rough derivation: GiveWell values preventing a young child's death at about 116 years of doubled income, and that death costs roughly 55–65 years of life in sub-Saharan Africa, so one healthy year is worth about 2. This ignores GiveWell's weighting by age and treats a year lived with illness like a year lost to death. The number and its 1–4 range are ours, not GiveWell's.

rows.label: A day of disabling pain, as a share of a year of healthy life
rows.explainer:
Animal charities measure the suffering they prevent in days of pain, adjusted for how intense the pain is and for how much each species can suffer compared with a person. (Ambitious Impact calls these suffering-adjusted days; ACE uses them.) After that adjustment, one such day is as bad as one day of a person's disabling pain.

This setting says how bad a day of disabling pain is. By default it costs as much as losing 0.4 of a day of healthy life (range 0.1 to a full day), which is 0.11% of a healthy year. Nobody publishes an official rate, so this is the least grounded number on the site, and it often decides whether animal charities rank above or below global health.

rows.label: One more point of life satisfaction for a year, in years of doubled income
rows.technical: Units of value per WELLBY (wellbeing-adjusted life year)
rows.explainer:
The Happier Lives Institute measures good done as gains in life satisfaction on a 0–10 scale. This says how many years of doubled income one point more, for one person for one year, is worth.

The default makes both evaluators agree on GiveDirectly: HLI estimates 7.55 points-for-a-year per $1,000 given, GiveWell 8.7 years of doubled income per $1,000, so one point is worth about 1.15. That assumes both measure GiveDirectly's good equally well, which is contested: GiveWell has been sceptical of some life-satisfaction estimates, HLI of some income-based ones. The wide range is ours.

rows.label: Weight on animal suffering, beyond each species' capacity to suffer
rows.explainer: Animal suffering is already scaled by how much each species can suffer compared with a person (its "welfare range"). At 1 you take those estimates at face value. Below 1 you count animal suffering for less still, for example because you're unsure animals feel pain the way people do, or because you give people more weight for other reasons.

rows.label: Weight on raising incomes, compared with health and lives
rows.technical: Units of value per unit of ln(consumption)
rows.explainer:
How much income gains count against everything else. Income gains are valued by how much they multiply someone's income, so doubling a poor person's income counts the same as doubling a rich person's. The default, 1.44, is GiveWell's: at that weight, doubling one person's income for a year is worth exactly one year of doubled income, the yardstick everything else is measured in.

Raise it and income programmes such as cash transfers count for more against saving lives and adding healthy years; lower it and they count for less. The low and high ends are the ±25% range GiveWell itself uses.

rows.label: Saving a life compared with raising incomes, relative to GiveWell
rows.technical: Life value multiplier on GiveWell's moral weights
rows.explainer:
GiveWell counts preventing a young child's death as worth about 116 years of doubled income, with similar weights for other ages. Those weights come from donor surveys, a survey of people in Ghana and Kenya, and staff judgment.

This multiplies all of them at once. At 1 you use GiveWell's weights; above 1 saving lives counts for more against raising incomes, below 1 for less. The 0.6–1.4 range is ours.

rows.label: How much less good done a year from now counts
rows.explainer:
How much less a benefit a year from now counts than the same benefit today, compounding each year. GiveWell and ACE both use 4%.

It applies where a model discounts explicitly (ACE's cage-free campaigns). GiveWell's GiveDirectly model has the 4% built into its later-years income figures, so changing this doesn't affect it yet.

uov.label: GiveWell units of value
uov.explainer: One unit = doubling one person's consumption for one year.

sad.label: suffering-adjusted days averted
sad.explainer: Days of animal suffering averted, weighted by pain intensity and species welfare range (Ambitious Impact).

people_reached.label: people reached
people_reached.explainer: People who saw or took part in a program. Says nothing about changes in behaviour, so it isn't converted into good done.

paper.label: peer-reviewed papers
paper.explainer: Peer-reviewed research papers produced. Research value depends on what it enables later, which nobody has quantified for this field.

wellby.label: wellbeing-adjusted life years
wellby.explainer: One point of life satisfaction (0–10) for one person for one year. Used by the Happier Lives Institute.

animals_spared.label: animals spared
animals_spared.explainer: Farmed animals spared from life in factory farming, ACE's 2014–2017 headline unit. It counts animals of every species alike and isn't weighted by suffering, so it isn't converted into good done.

daly.label: DALYs averted
daly.explainer: Disability-adjusted life years averted. Converted into units of value with the shared DALY exchange rate.
